title: The Library of Alexandria

cards.h: The library that became a legend
cards.b:
The Library of Alexandria, in Egypt, was one of the most famous places of learning in the ancient world. It was part of a research centre called the Mouseion, and it collected scrolls from across the Mediterranean.

Its story is part fact and part legend. The question of what was lost, and why, still fascinates readers and historians.

The Ptolemaic kings of Egypt founded the library around 300 BCE, under Ptolemy I or Ptolemy II. They bought and copied books and sent ships to borrow scrolls from other cities. Some books were said to be taken from visitors who were searched.

The library grew to hold many hundreds of thousands of scrolls at its height, though the exact number is uncertain. It was a place where scholars from around the Mediterranean lived and worked.

Scholars at Alexandria made major advances. Eratosthenes, who ran the library, measured the size of the Earth by comparing shadows in Alexandria and Syene. Euclid, who taught mathematics there, wrote his Elements, which shaped geometry for centuries.

The city was a place of debate, poetry and medicine. Its scholars edited Homer, catalogued literature and studied the stars.

Strabo (c. 64 BCE – c. 24 CE)

The Greek geographer Strabo visited Alexandria and described the Mouseion. He wrote of its shared dining hall, its scholars and their salaries paid by the state.

His account is one of the few eyewitness descriptions of the institution.
The library did not disappear in one night. It faded over centuries, through wars, neglect and changing priorities.

A popular story says that Julius Caesar set fire to the library in 48 BCE and destroyed its books. The image of a great fire is dramatic and widely repeated.

Historians argue the fire was real but limited. Roman writers mention books being lost in fighting near the harbour. The library may have survived for centuries after that, so the single fire story is probably exaggerated.

A later legend claims that the Caliph Omar ordered the books burned as fuel for the city's baths. The story appears in writings of the 1200s, centuries after the events. Historians treat it as a legend, not a record.

The legend shows how later writers used the library as a symbol. It is a warning about the fragility of knowledge.

Much of the ancient world we know survives through copies made in Alexandria. Scholars there created standard texts of Homer and the tragedians, and their editions helped preserve the Greek literary canon.

Historians argue that the real loss was not one fire, but the slow decline of funding, copying and interest over centuries. What survived depended on luck and on a few people who kept copying.

The Serapeum, a temple in Alexandria that held a daughter library, was destroyed in 391 CE during a campaign against pagan sites. Some books may have been lost then, though the evidence is limited.

By the time of the Arab conquest in 642, the library was no longer the great institution it had been. The question of how much was lost is still open.

cards.h: The idea of a universal library
cards.b:
The Library of Alexandria became a model for later collections, from the libraries of Baghdad and Cordoba to modern national libraries. Its ideal of gathering all knowledge in one place still inspires projects today.

The lesson is double-edged. The ideal of a universal collection is powerful, but it depends on money, politics and the survival of institutions.

Alexandria's Ptolemies were in contact with India. Ashoka's rock edicts, carved in the mid-200s BCE, name Greek kings in the west who received Buddhist envoys, among them a ruler called Ptolemy.

So the library was one node in a wider world of exchange. Greek learning and Indian religion met in the same century, and both left records of the contact.

Five things to remember
  1. The library was part of the Mouseion, a research centre.
  2. The Ptolemies founded it around 300 BCE.
  3. Eratosthenes measured the Earth using shadows.
  4. The fire of 48 BCE was real but limited.
  5. The story of Omar burning the books is a later legend.
Think about it
  • Why do lost libraries become legends?
  • What makes a body of knowledge survive for centuries?
